title.v: What Web3 Mobile App Development Actually Involves

c.v: A Web3 mobile app is a native or cross-platform iOS/Android application where at least part of the product runs on a blockchain. That part can be user identity, asset ownership, payments or business logic enforced by smart contracts. The phone shows the interface. A wallet, either inside the app or a separate one, holds the keys that authorize actions. The blockchain records the result.

blocks.alt: Diagram of Web3 mobile app architecture: mobile client, wallet and signing layer, backend and indexer, blockchain network

c.v: Building one is not the same as wrapping a website in an app. A production Web3 mobile product usually has four layers that must work together:
Mobile client

rows.v: Screens, navigation, local security, deep links, notifications
Swift/SwiftUI, Kotlin/Jetpack Compose, React Native or Flutter

c.v: Wallet and signing

rows.v: Creates or connects a wallet, signs messages and transactions
WalletConnect (Reown AppKit), MetaMask Connect, embedded wallet SDKs, smart accounts

c.v: Backend and indexing

rows.v: Fast reads, history, search, push notifications, protected API keys
Node.js services, The Graph or Goldsky indexers, webhooks, PostgreSQL/Redis

c.v: Blockchain

rows.v: Ethereum and EVM networks (Arbitrum, Base, Optimism, Polygon, Avalanche), Solana

c.v: How a Web3 mobile app differs from a traditional app
Identity is a key, not a password.
Users prove who they are by signing with a wallet. Nobody can reset a lost self-custody key, so recovery design matters from day one.
Assets live on a public ledger.
A user's tokens or NFTs exist outside your database and can be used in other apps. That is valuable, but it also means you can't quietly edit balances.
Actions have cost and latency.
Writes need network fees and take time to confirm. The interface has to show
pending
confirmed
and
failed
honestly instead of pretending everything is instant.
Some logic can't be patched with an app update.
Deployed smart contracts follow their own upgrade rules, separate from your App Store release cycle. Mobile releases and contract upgrades have to be planned together.
Custom Web3 Mobile Application Development

New products built from scratch: product discovery, contract design, wallet strategy, UI/UX, mobile engineering, backend, testing and store launch. Use this when the blockchain is central to the product, for example a non-custodial trading app, a tokenized loyalty program or an on-chain game companion app.
Adding Web3 Features to an Existing Mobile App

Many teams already have a working app and want to add wallets, token rewards, NFT ownership or crypto payments without a rebuild. We audit your current architecture and decide which features really need on-chain state. Then we add a blockchain layer: wallet SDKs in the client, plus a backend service that connects your existing APIs to the chain. Your current accounts system keeps working, and wallet linking becomes an option rather than a forced migration.
Mobile dApp Development
Mobile front ends for protocols and on-chain products: DEX and swap interfaces, lending and staking dashboards, DAO voting, token-gated communities. A mobile dApp
asks
a wallet to sign. It doesn't need to hold keys itself, which keeps your security scope and regulatory exposure smaller.
Mobile Crypto Wallet Development
If the product
is

the wallet (it holds keys, signs, and shows balances across chains), the security and compliance work goes much deeper. We build non-custodial mobile wallets with secure key storage, recovery, multi-chain support and WalletConnect support so users can connect to other dApps.
DeFi Mobile App Development

DeFi on a phone mostly comes down to information design and careful signing. We build apps that show positions, yields and health factors from indexed data. Users get warnings before a risky action, such as a loan approaching its liquidation threshold. Swaps, deposits and withdrawals are built as transactions with simulated outcomes shown before the user signs. Integrations can target existing protocols or your own contracts.
NFT Mobile App Development

Galleries that load quickly, minting flows, and marketplace front ends for ERC-721 and ERC-1155 assets. Metadata is resolved from IPFS or Arweave and cached through a CDN so images don't stall on slow gateways. We also handle the App Store rules on NFTs (more below), which affect where purchase buttons can appear and what NFT ownership is allowed to unlock.
Crypto Payments in Mobile Apps

Stablecoin checkout, wallet-to-wallet transfers, QR payment requests, payment links and merchant flows. Payment status is confirmed by the backend before an order is fulfilled. Where users need to buy crypto first, we integrate a fiat on-ramp provider that meets your compliance needs.

title.v: Wallet Integration: How Your Users Connect, Sign In and Pay

c.v: The wallet decision shapes your onboarding, your security model, your compliance position and your costs. We help you make it early, because it's expensive to change after launch.
External Wallet Connection with WalletConnect, MetaMask, Coinbase and Phantom
Crypto-native users already have wallets and want to use them. On mobile, the connection doesn't happen inside a browser extension. It happens between two apps:

blocks.alt: Mobile wallet connection flow using WalletConnect deep links between a dApp and a wallet app

c.v: Your app creates a session request and opens the user's wallet with a deep link or universal link. On desktop it shows a QR code.
The user approves the connection in the wallet.
The wallet returns the user to your app, and the session stays alive through an encrypted relay. Later signing requests reopen the wallet briefly for approval.
We implement this with
Reown AppKit
(the current WalletConnect SDK family, formerly Web3Modal), which has SDKs for Swift, Kotlin, React Native and Flutter. Where supported, we use
Link Mode
, which routes requests through verified universal links and app links so app switching is faster and more reliable. We also integrate
MetaMask Connect
and
Base Account
(Coinbase's successor to the Coinbase Wallet SDK) for React Native apps. On Android, Solana apps can use
Mobile Wallet Adapter
to talk to wallets such as Phantom and Solflare. Solana Mobile doesn't support it on iOS, so iOS Solana apps need a different design, usually an embedded wallet.

The details that make or break this flow are mostly about the return trip. The app should confirm the session from the wallet's response, not just assume success because the user came back. It has to recover when iOS or Android kills the app in the background, and it has to handle users who have several wallets installed. We test these paths on real devices, not just simulators.
Embedded Wallets with Email, Social and Passkey Login

Most mainstream users don't have a wallet and won't install one to try your app. Embedded wallets create one inside your app when the user signs in with email, Google or Apple, or a passkey. They never see a seed phrase unless they choose to export their key.

Embedded wallet providers secure keys in different ways. Some split keys into shares (MPC), some use secure hardware environments, and some use smart accounts controlled by passkeys. They also differ on pricing, chain support, export options and vendor lock-in. We have integration experience with providers such as Privy, Dynamic, Turnkey, MetaMask Embedded Wallets (formerly Web3Auth) and Coinbase's CDP Embedded Wallets. We recommend one based on your chains, your custody position and your expected wallet volume.
Smart Accounts, Gas Sponsorship and Passkeys
Two blockchain changes make mobile onboarding much easier than it was a few years ago:
Account abstraction (ERC-4337) and EIP-7702.
These turn a wallet into a programmable account. Your app can
sponsor network fees
through a paymaster, so a new user can mint or claim without first buying ETH. It can
batch
steps into one approval (for example, "approve and swap" becomes a single tap). It can also add
spending limits and session keys
for games and frequent small actions. EIP-7702 has been live on Ethereum since the May 2025 Pectra upgrade and brings these features to existing wallet addresses.
Passkey-controlled accounts.

Since Ethereum's Fusaka upgrade (December 2025), the network can cheaply verify the P-256 signatures that iPhone and Android secure hardware produce. Many Layer 2 networks already supported this. The result is a wallet whose signing key never leaves the phone's secure hardware and is unlocked with Face ID or a fingerprint, with no seed phrase to write down.
These features are EVM-specific. On Solana we use different tools to reach similar results, such as fee payers for sponsored transactions.
Which Wallet Model Fits Your App?

blocks.alt: Comparison of embedded wallet onboarding with email or passkey versus connecting an external crypto wallet

rows.v: External wallets via WalletConnect and MetaMask Connect
App switching on every signature; fewer mainstream signups
Provider fees and dependency; recovery design
Embedded wallet by default, "connect your own wallet" as an option
Two flows to build, test and support
You are building the wallet itself
Highest security, audit and store-policy scope

c.v: Many crypto losses start with a user approving something they couldn't read. On a small screen that risk is higher, so we treat the signing screen as the most important screen in the app:

blocks.alt: Mobile transaction signing screen showing readable approval details, network fee in dollars and confirmation status

c.v: Readable requests.
Wherever possible we use typed, structured signing (EIP-712). Wallets then show fields like "Spend up to 500 USDC on Exchange X" instead of a block of hex.
Simulation before signing.
The app previews the expected outcome, such as tokens out, tokens in and approvals granted, and flags unusual results such as unlimited token approvals.
Fees in plain money.
Network fees are estimated from current conditions (EIP-1559 base and priority fees on EVM chains) and shown in the user's currency before they approve.
Honest status.
Every transaction moves through visible states:
awaiting signature → submitted → confirmed
, or
failed / dropped
, with retry or speed-up options. We never show "Success" just because a transaction was broadcast.
Sign-in with a wallet.

Where the app has accounts, we implement Sign-In with Ethereum (EIP-4361): a one-time signed message with a nonce and expiry, verified by your backend. Smart-account users are supported through EIP-1271 signature checks.

title.v: Smart Contract and Blockchain Network Integration

c.v: Reading On-Chain Data Fast
A phone can't scan a blockchain. Loading a user's full transfer history or NFT collection straight from a node is slow and drains data and battery. We split reads into two kinds:
Live, authoritative reads
, such as balances, allowances or a contract's current state, go through RPC providers like Alchemy, Infura or QuickNode, with failover between providers.
History and aggregates
, such as activity feeds, portfolio values or collection lists, come from an indexer such as subgraphs on The Graph Network or Goldsky. Indexers turn contract events into fast, queryable APIs.
The app caches results and shows when data was last updated, so users always know how fresh a number is.
Writing to Smart Contracts

We integrate the mobile app with your existing contracts or with contracts we develop: token standards (ERC-20, ERC-721, ERC-1155), staking, escrow, governance and marketplace logic. Typed contract bindings generated from ABIs keep the app, backend and contracts in sync when a contract changes. Before we connect anything to mainnet, we test it against local forks and public testnets.
Multi-Chain Mobile Applications
Supporting several networks means more than adding RPC URLs. We design multi-chain apps so that:
each network has its own configuration (contract addresses, confirmation rules, explorer links and fee tokens), so adding a chain is a configuration change, not a rewrite
accounts and chains are identified with chain-agnostic standards (CAIP-2 and CAIP-10), which current wallet SDKs use for multi-chain sessions
users always see which network they are on, and the app asks the wallet to switch networks instead of failing silently
EVM and Solana code paths are separated where their signing and data models differ
moving assets between networks is shown as one guided flow, with bridge time and fees displayed up front, instead of sending users to a separate bridge site
fees can be paid in stablecoins or sponsored by the app where the network supports it, so users don't need a gas token for every chain they touch
Networks we work with:
Ethereum, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, Polygon, Avalanche, BNB Chain and Solana. Other EVM-compatible networks can be added on request.
The Backend Between Your App and the Chain
Most production Web3 apps need a backend, even though the core logic is decentralized. Ours typically handles:
Push notifications for on-chain events.

iOS and Android don't let apps stay connected to a blockchain node in the background. A backend listener or provider webhook watches for events and delivers them through Apple Push Notification service and Firebase Cloud Messaging. Typical events are incoming transfers, confirmed transactions, liquidation warnings and NFT sales.
Protected credentials.
Paid RPC and API keys stay on the server instead of shipping inside an app binary that can be decompiled.
Off-chain data.
Profiles, media, search, analytics and anything personal stay off-chain, because data on a public chain can't be deleted.
Webhooks and reconciliation
for payments and orders, so business systems act only on confirmed transactions.

title.v: Native vs Cross-Platform Web3 App Development

c.v: There isn't one right framework for every Web3 app. The best choice depends on how much of the Web3 toolset you need, how security-critical signing is, and whether you share code with a web dApp.

blocks.alt: Comparison of React Native, Flutter and native Swift/Kotlin for Web3 mobile app development

c.v: React Native Web3 Development

React Native has the broadest Web3 SDK support of any mobile framework. That includes viem and wagmi, Reown AppKit, MetaMask Connect, Base Account, and most embedded-wallet providers. Teams that also run a TypeScript web dApp can share contract bindings, validation and business logic across web and mobile. Current React Native releases run only on the New Architecture. We handle the setup Web3 libraries need, such as secure random number polyfills and native crypto modules, so cryptographic work doesn't slow the interface. This is our default for most mobile dApps.
Flutter Web3 Development

Flutter is a strong choice for highly branded, animation-heavy interfaces with one rendering engine on both platforms. Its Web3 toolset is narrower. WalletConnect is available through Reown's Flutter SDK, but Dart blockchain libraries are mostly community-maintained, and fewer embedded-wallet providers offer Flutter SDKs. We recommend Flutter when the Web3 part of the app is well defined (wallet connection plus contract reads and writes) and the visual experience is a priority.
Native iOS (Swift, SwiftUI) and Android (Kotlin, Jetpack Compose)

Native development gives direct access to platform security (Keychain, Secure Enclave, Android Keystore and StrongBox), passkeys, widgets and the best runtime performance. It is the safer choice for wallets and other key-holding apps. On Android it is also the natural fit for Solana Mobile Wallet Adapter and Seed Vault integration. The trade-off is two codebases to build and maintain.

title.v: Web3 Mobile Security: Keys, Biometrics and App Hardening

c.v: Private Key Protection on iOS and Android
Wallet security is often described inaccurately. The secure chips in iPhones (Secure Enclave) and many Android phones (TEE or StrongBox) can only generate and use
keys. Ethereum and Solana keys use different cryptography (secp256k1 and ed25519), so they can't be stored
inside
that hardware directly.

blocks.alt: How a mobile wallet protects private keys: encryption with a Secure Enclave or Android Keystore key and biometric unlock

c.v: When an app holds a self-custody key, we use the pattern Apple and Google intend for this case:
The wallet key is encrypted with a key that never leaves the device's secure hardware.
The encrypted key is stored in the iOS Keychain or with an Android Keystore-protected key. It is marked
device-only
, so it isn't copied to backups or other devices.
Decryption requires a fresh Face ID, Touch ID or fingerprint check that is tied to the key itself, not a simple yes/no check that a compromised device could skip.
Where the chain supports it, a passkey-controlled smart account removes the exported key entirely, because the signing key never leaves the secure hardware.
Biometric Authentication That Actually Protects Assets

Biometrics should guard specific actions: unlocking the key, approving a large transfer, viewing a recovery phrase, changing security settings. They shouldn't just be a lock screen on app launch. We bind biometric checks to keys with platform APIs (LocalAuthentication with Keychain access control on iOS, BiometricPrompt with auth-bound Keystore keys on Android). We also design fallbacks for when the user's biometrics change.
Mobile App Hardening
We build and test against the
OWASP Mobile Application Security Verification Standard (MASVS)
and check the risks in the
OWASP Mobile Top 10
. For a Web3 app that typically means:
no secrets in the app binary
certificate pinning for backend APIs
secure local storage
screenshot and screen-recording protection on recovery-phrase screens
clipboard hygiene for wallet addresses
phishing protection for any in-app dApp browser
jailbreak and root signals used for risk scoring
Smart Contract Security and Independent Audits

Mobile security is wasted if the contracts behind it are vulnerable. Our contract work includes unit, fuzz and invariant testing, established libraries such as OpenZeppelin, and an independent third-party audit before mainnet deployment. We don't audit our own code.

title.v: App Store and Google Play Readiness

c.v: Plenty of Web3 apps work perfectly and still get rejected. We plan for store policy during discovery, not after submission:
Apple:
wallet apps must be published by a developer enrolled as an
organization
, not an individual. Exchange features may only be offered where the app has the right licensing. NFTs can be shown to the people who own them, but
owning an NFT can't unlock features or functionality
in the app. Outside the US storefront, links or buttons that send users to non-in-app-purchase NFT sales aren't allowed.
Google Play:
crypto exchanges and software wallets must complete Play's
Financial Features declaration
. Exchanges and custodial wallets need licences in many countries and must drop countries where they aren't licensed. Non-custodial wallets confirm their status instead.
Regulation beyond the stores:

if your company holds user funds or runs an exchange, it may need licences or registration, such as MiCA authorization in the EU or money transmission rules in the US. KYC/AML checks for fiat on-ramps are usually handled by the on-ramp provider. We design the custody model with your legal counsel; we are engineers, not lawyers.

These rules affect product decisions: whether you are custodial or non-custodial, where purchase buttons go, what token ownership is allowed to do, and which countries you launch in. We flag the issues early and design compliant alternatives. Final approval is always Apple's and Google's decision, so we never promise it.

title.v: Mobile UX for Web3: Onboarding, Recovery and Performance

c.v: Progressive onboarding.
Let people explore before they create a wallet. Ask for a signature only when an action needs one.
Recovery users will actually complete.
Cloud-encrypted backups, social or guardian recovery, or passkey sync. Each has trade-offs that we explain in plain language during design.
Language without jargon.
"Approve spending" instead of "setApprovalForAll", and network names instead of chain IDs.
Offline and poor-network handling.
Cached balances with a "last updated" time, queued actions that ask for confirmation again when the app comes back online, and retries that never send the same transaction twice.
Performance budgets.
Fast app start, lazy-loaded NFT media, and cryptographic work kept off the main UI thread.
Accessibility.
Screen reader labels on addresses and amounts, and support for large text settings. Financial apps have to be readable.

title.v: Our Web3 Mobile App Development Process

blocks.alt: Six-step Web3 mobile app development process from discovery to store launch and support

c.v: 1. Discovery and Architecture (typically 1–2 weeks)
We define your users, the on-chain vs off-chain split, the wallet model, target networks, store-policy risks and the framework choice.
You receive:
an architecture document, a wallet and custody recommendation, a fixed-price scope and a delivery plan.
2. UX and Interface Design
Wireframes and clickable prototypes for onboarding, signing, transaction status and recovery. These are the flows where Web3 apps lose most users. We test them before engineering starts.
3. Smart Contract and Backend Build
Contracts are developed and tested. Indexers, notification services and APIs are built alongside them, so the mobile team works against real interfaces early.
4. Mobile Development
Iterative builds delivered to your team through TestFlight and Google Play internal testing. Wallet flows are exercised on real devices with real wallet apps.
5. Security Review and Testing
This stage covers:
mobile security testing against MASVS
an independent smart contract audit
end-to-end tests on public testnets and local mainnet forks
testing on a range of real iPhones and Android phones, including older devices and slow networks
failure testing for dropped and replaced transactions, network switches, wallet app updates, and the operating system terminating the app mid-signature
6. Store Submission, Launch and Ongoing Support

We prepare store listings, privacy declarations and the financial-features forms, then support you through review. After launch we monitor transactions and infrastructure, update wallet SDKs as they change, and plan app releases alongside any contract upgrades.
Every engagement has one accountable project lead, and core deliverables are scoped at a fixed price after discovery. We don't use open-ended hourly billing.

c.v: We design the system, not just the screens.

Wallet model, contract interfaces, indexing, backend and mobile client are planned together in one architecture document. Onboarding, signing and data speed problems usually come from gaps between those layers.
We pick onboarding based on your users.

We don't push every user to MetaMask, and we don't force an embedded-wallet vendor on crypto-native users. We recommend the wallet model that matches your audience and custody position, then build a fallback path.
We describe security accurately.
We won't tell you a seed phrase "lives in the Secure Enclave". We explain exactly how keys are protected on each platform, test against OWASP MASVS, and use independent auditors for contracts.
We plan for store review from the start.
Apple and Google policy is a discovery item, not a surprise at submission.
Commercial terms are clear.
You get a free strategy call, an NDA before the first meeting, fixed-price scoping after discovery, and one accountable project lead.
We support the app after launch.
Wallet SDKs, chain upgrades and store policies keep changing. We keep your app current and plan contract upgrades and mobile releases together.
What is Web3 mobile app development?

It is building iOS and Android apps that use a blockchain for some core functions, usually user identity through a wallet, ownership of tokens or NFTs, payments, or rules enforced by smart contracts. Development covers the mobile client, wallet integration, smart contract interaction, a supporting backend and indexing, and App Store and Google Play compliance.
Can Web3 apps run on both iOS and Android?

Yes. Cross-platform frameworks such as React Native and Flutter ship one codebase to both platforms, and native Swift and Kotlin apps are built separately for each. Most wallet tools, including WalletConnect, support both platforms. A notable exception is Solana's Mobile Wallet Adapter, which works only on Android, so Solana apps on iOS usually use embedded wallets instead.
How does a mobile app connect to a crypto wallet?
There are two main ways. With an
external wallet

, the app sends a connection request to an installed wallet such as MetaMask or Phantom through a deep link (usually with WalletConnect). The user approves in the wallet and returns to the app. With an
embedded wallet
, the app creates a wallet for the user during sign-up with email, social login or a passkey, so no separate app is needed.
How are private keys secured in a mobile app?

For self-custody wallets, the key is encrypted with a key held in the phone's secure hardware (Secure Enclave on iPhone, Keystore or StrongBox on Android). It is stored as device-only, and decryption requires a fresh biometric check. Embedded wallets may instead split keys across parties (MPC) or use passkey-controlled smart accounts where the signing key never leaves secure hardware. A mobile dApp that connects to an external wallet never holds the user's key at all.
Should I use Flutter or React Native for a Web3 mobile app?

React Native usually wins for Web3 because it has the widest choice of wallet, embedded-wallet and blockchain libraries, and it can share TypeScript code with a web dApp. Flutter is a good fit when the interface is highly branded and the blockchain features are well defined, because its WalletConnect support is solid but its wider Web3 library choice is smaller. For wallets that hold keys, native Swift and Kotlin give the most direct access to device security.
How much does it cost to build a Web3 mobile app?

Based on ClickMasters' published cost guides, adding wallet connection to an existing app typically starts around $17,000. A full iOS and Android app for a Web3 product typically costs $60,000–$140,000, and a multi-chain non-custodial wallet can reach $165,000. Audits and third-party service fees are extra. A discovery phase produces a fixed-price quote for your scope.
How long does it take to build a Web3 mobile app?

Wallet integration into an existing app can take a few weeks. A complete mobile app for a Web3 product typically takes about 10–16 weeks, and multi-chain wallets 14–22 weeks. Allow extra time for an independent smart contract audit and for App Store and Google Play review.
Can you convert our existing mobile app into a Web3 app?

Usually, yes, without a rebuild. We add wallet SDKs to your app and a backend service that connects your existing systems to the blockchain. Only the features that benefit from being on-chain move there, such as asset ownership, rewards or payments. Existing user accounts can stay, with wallet linking offered as an option.
Do my users need a crypto wallet to use the app?

Not necessarily. With embedded wallets, users sign in with email, social login or a passkey and get a wallet automatically. With gas sponsorship, they don't even need crypto to pay network fees. Users who already have wallets can still connect them.
Will Apple and Google approve a crypto or NFT app?

They approve many, but there are firm rules. Apple requires wallet apps to come from registered organizations, requires licensing for exchange features, and doesn't allow NFT ownership to unlock app functionality. Google Play requires a financial features declaration, and licences for exchanges and custodial wallets in many countries. We design around these rules from discovery, but approval is always the store's decision.
Which blockchains can a Web3 mobile app support?

Most commonly Ethereum and EVM networks such as Arbitrum, Base, Optimism, Polygon, Avalanche and BNB Chain, plus Solana. A well-designed app treats each network as configuration, so new chains can be added later without rewriting the app.
Who maintains the app after launch?

We offer ongoing support: monitoring transactions and infrastructure, updating wallet and blockchain SDKs, adapting to new OS and store-policy changes, and coordinating mobile releases with smart contract upgrades.

faq.q: Can Web3 apps run on both iOS and Android?

c.v: Yes. Cross-platform frameworks such as React Native and Flutter ship one codebase to both platforms, and native Swift and Kotlin apps are built separately for each. Most wallet tools, including WalletConnect, support both platforms. A notable exception is Solana's Mobile Wallet Adapter, which works only on Android, so Solana apps on iOS usually use embedded wallets instead.

faq.q: How does a mobile app connect to a crypto wallet?

c.v: There are two main ways. With an
external wallet

, the app sends a connection request to an installed wallet such as MetaMask or Phantom through a deep link (usually with WalletConnect). The user approves in the wallet and returns to the app. With an
embedded wallet
, the app creates a wallet for the user during sign-up with email, social login or a passkey, so no separate app is needed.

faq.q: How are private keys secured in a mobile app?

c.v: For self-custody wallets, the key is encrypted with a key held in the phone's secure hardware (Secure Enclave on iPhone, Keystore or StrongBox on Android). It is stored as device-only, and decryption requires a fresh biometric check. Embedded wallets may instead split keys across parties (MPC) or use passkey-controlled smart accounts where the signing key never leaves secure hardware. A mobile dApp that connects to an external wallet never holds the user's key at all.

faq.q: Should I use Flutter or React Native for a Web3 mobile app?

c.v: React Native usually wins for Web3 because it has the widest choice of wallet, embedded-wallet and blockchain libraries, and it can share TypeScript code with a web dApp. Flutter is a good fit when the interface is highly branded and the blockchain features are well defined, because its WalletConnect support is solid but its wider Web3 library choice is smaller. For wallets that hold keys, native Swift and Kotlin give the most direct access to device security.

faq.q: How much does it cost to build a Web3 mobile app?

c.v: Based on ClickMasters' published cost guides, adding wallet connection to an existing app typically starts around $17,000. A full iOS and Android app for a Web3 product typically costs $60,000–$140,000, and a multi-chain non-custodial wallet can reach $165,000. Audits and third-party service fees are extra. A discovery phase produces a fixed-price quote for your scope.

faq.q: How long does it take to build a Web3 mobile app?

c.v: Wallet integration into an existing app can take a few weeks. A complete mobile app for a Web3 product typically takes about 10–16 weeks, and multi-chain wallets 14–22 weeks. Allow extra time for an independent smart contract audit and for App Store and Google Play review.

faq.q: Can you convert our existing mobile app into a Web3 app?

c.v: Usually, yes, without a rebuild. We add wallet SDKs to your app and a backend service that connects your existing systems to the blockchain. Only the features that benefit from being on-chain move there, such as asset ownership, rewards or payments. Existing user accounts can stay, with wallet linking offered as an option.

faq.q: Do my users need a crypto wallet to use the app?

c.v: Not necessarily. With embedded wallets, users sign in with email, social login or a passkey and get a wallet automatically. With gas sponsorship, they don't even need crypto to pay network fees. Users who already have wallets can still connect them.

faq.q: Will Apple and Google approve a crypto or NFT app?

c.v: They approve many, but there are firm rules. Apple requires wallet apps to come from registered organizations, requires licensing for exchange features, and doesn't allow NFT ownership to unlock app functionality. Google Play requires a financial features declaration, and licences for exchanges and custodial wallets in many countries. We design around these rules from discovery, but approval is always the store's decision.

faq.q: Which blockchains can a Web3 mobile app support?

c.v: Most commonly Ethereum and EVM networks such as Arbitrum, Base, Optimism, Polygon, Avalanche and BNB Chain, plus Solana. A well-designed app treats each network as configuration, so new chains can be added later without rewriting the app.

faq.q: Who maintains the app after launch?

c.v: We offer ongoing support: monitoring transactions and infrastructure, updating wallet and blockchain SDKs, adapting to new OS and store-policy changes, and coordinating mobile releases with smart contract upgrades.
